Powered by water or wind, these mills ground grain into flour, providing the essential ingredient for bread, a staple of everyday life. But they were more than just places of work – they were economic hubs that helped shape Canada's growth. Many still stand today as heritage sites, offering a glimpse into the ingenuity that helped early settlers (and their sourdough starters) thrive.
GRUNT: If Nova Scotia had an official dessert, it might just be Blueberry Grunt. This timeless combination of wild blueberries and crumbly biscuits is an iconic East Coast classic! This cobbler style dessert is great all year round, but it's best with fresh blueberries in the summer!
GUEST: Twenty-five years ago, nearly 6,600 passengers became unexpected guests in Newfoundland after 38 planes were diverted following the 9/11 attacks. Local residents in Gander and surrounding communities welcomed the “come from aways” into their homes and communities, providing food, shelter, friendship and remarkable Newfoundland hospitality. Their story inspired the hit musical [Come From Away](https://comefromaway.com/).
GUIDE: Girl Guides of Canada started on September 7, 1910, and Canada was among the founding members of the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts (WAGGGS) in 1928. Some well-known former Girl Guides include: Queen Elizabeth II, Margaret Atwood, Celine Dion, Sarah McLachlan, and Dr. Roberta Bondar, who juggled Girl Guide cookies in space!
GUILD: A guild is an association of artisans and merchants who oversee the practice of their craft/trade in a particular territory. Some notable guilds in Canada include the Canadian Merchant Service Guild, Canadian Media Guild, Writers Guild, Directors Guild, Playwrights Guild, Screen Composers Guild, and various Quilters, Spinners & Weavers Guilds!
HATCH: Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen is set to make history on [Artemis II](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/missions/artemis-ii/mission.asp), becoming the first Canadian to fly to the Moon. The Orion spacecraft’s crew module hatch is crucial to the mission: it seals the astronauts in for launch, keeps them safe during re-entry at nearly 40,000 km/h, and will be used by recovery teams after splashdown. Every hatch is a gateway to exploration, marking Canada’s bold step into lunar missions and deep-space adventures.
HAWKS: The [Golden Hawks](https://cahf.ca/royal-canadian-air-force-golden-hawks/) were a Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aerobatic flying team established in 1959 to celebrate the 35th anniversary of the RCAF and the "Golden" 50th anniversary of Canadian flight, which began with the AEA Silver Dart in 1909.
HEIST: Over the course of several months in 2011 and 2012, a team of thieves stole approximately 2,700 tonnes of maple syrup from a strategic maple syrup reserve maintained in Quebec. The theft has been popularly dubbed as the [Great Canadian Maple Syrup Heist](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/great-canadian-maple-syrup-heist). At the time of the heist, the stolen maple syrup was valued at nearly $18 million. The heist may be one of the largest thefts in Canadian history.
HELLO: Happy Victoria Day! 👑 [Hello! Canada](https://www.hellomagazine.com/ca/) magazine is a Canadian entertainment magazine that launched in 2006 by Rogers Media. Published weekly, it covers the latest celebrity and royal news from around the world. Hello! Canada has become a beloved publication among Canadian readers, so much so that it is the top-selling magazine on Canadian newsstands and is a leading entertainment brand online!
HERON: Great blue herons are Canada's most widespread heron and are found from the Maritimes to British Columbia. As the largest heron in North America, the great blue heron stands about one metre tall.
HIDES: On May 15, we mark [Moose Hide Campaign Day](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/), a national day of action for the Indigenous-led grassroots movement to engage men and boys in ending violence towards women and children. The Moose Hide Campaign began with a small patch of moose hide, worn as a symbol of commitment to safety and healing. Today, millions across Canada wear these hides to stand up against gender-based violence. To support them in igniting powerful change, please consider [donating to the Moose Hide Campaign](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/donate/) today.
HOCUS: From 1981 to 1987, the Canadian children’s show Today’s Special brought magic to the screen for over 120 episodes. Set in a Toronto department store, the magic words “Hocus Pocus Alimagocus!” would bring Jeff the mannequin to life! The adventures of Jeff, Jodie, Sam Crenshaw, and Muffy Mouse delighted generations of viewers and made everyday moments feel truly magical.
HONEY: Canadian honey is recognized around the world for its high quality. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta produce 80% of Canada's honey crop. Canada is the world's sixth largest producer of honey. The average honey yield per hive in Canada is twice the world's average due to our long and warm summer days and a vast supply of nectar producing crops!
HOPPY: The hops used in Canadian beer bring bitterness, aroma and flavour to every brew, with hop-forward styles delivering an especially hoppy taste. On October 7, [Canadian Beer Day](https://canadianbeerday.ca/) celebrates the people, places and traditions behind Canadian beer, from local breweries to the pubs and restaurants where friends gather. Raise a glass to Canadian beer from coast to coast to coast!
HORSE: On April 30, 2002, a bill was passed into law by the Canadian Government making the Canadian horse an official symbol of Canada. The Canadian horse is known for its great strength and endurance, resilience, intelligence and good temper.
HOWLS: Wolves are known for their haunting howls, a form of communication used to signal territory, locate pack members, or coordinate hunting. In Canada, grey wolves roam vast regions from the forests of British Columbia to the tundra of Nunavut, and their howls echo across the wilderness, a timeless sound of the country’s wild landscapes.
HURON: With the longest shoreline of all of the Great Lakes, Lake Huron is one of the most unique lakes on Earth. It is the second largest of the Great Lakes, and the fourth largest lake in the world by surface area. The Huron Wendat are an Iroquoian-speaking nation in Canada, originally living along the St. Lawrence River and between Lake Huron and Lake Ontario.
HYDRA: Hydra was a crucial and secure radio communications link in Canada during the Second World War. Part of [Camp X](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/camp-x) (a training school for covert agents and a radio communications centre that operated on the shores of Lake Ontario between Whitby and Oshawa), Hydra sent and received Allied radio (including telegraph) signals from around the world. Hydra was the most sophisticated telecommunications centre of its time and was instrumental in coding/decoding information vital to the allied war effort.
HYDRO: Waterpower is Canada's most abundant source of clean and renewable electricity, providing more than 60% of Canada's total electricity today. Canada is the fourth largest generator of hydroelectricity in the world.
HYMNS: In Canada, Christmas hymns and carols play a significant role in holiday celebrations. The [Calgary Carol Festival](https://calgarycarolfestival.ca/) has become a cherished tradition, where choirs from across the city come together to perform festive hymns and carols and celebrate the season. The Festival of Carols by the Toronto Mendelssohn Choir is an annual event that brings together a blend of classical hymns, carols, and festive music. These hymns not only fill the air with holiday cheer, but also reflect Canada's deep-rooted love for music and community during the festive season​.
INDIE: Canada's indie scene is bursting with creativity! From homegrown musicians and filmmakers to independent game developers, Canadians are making waves with original, outside-the-box ideas. Whether it's a soulful song, a thought-provoking documentary, or a beautifully crafted game, Canada's indie creators prove that with passion and persistence, you don't need a blockbuster budget to make a big impact. The Great White North is full of independent spirit!
INFUSE: A grassroots idea with a big impact is gaining momentum in Canada. The “[Nanaimo Infusion](https://engageq.notion.site/infusion-2026),” sparked by Tod Maffin, takes place April 24-26, 2026, and invites visitors, especially U.S. healthcare workers, to experience life on Vancouver Island through a welcoming, community-driven weekend. What began as a creative tourism idea has since grown into a broader healthcare infusion initiative, helping connect skilled professionals with opportunities across Canada while showcasing the country’s quality of life.
INGOT: Gold is often cast into an ingot, a solid bar that makes the precious metal easier to store, transport and process. Canada has a long history of gold mining and ranked as the world’s fourth-largest gold producer in 2024, with Canadian mines producing nearly 200 tonnes. Ontario and Quebec accounted for 68% of the country’s gold production, making gold Canada’s most valuable mined commodity.
INLAY: Inlay artwork is a decorative technique that embeds one material within another to create patterns or designs. Indigenous artists in Canada have long used inlay to add meaning and beauty to their work, incorporating materials like shell, bone, stone, or metal into wood and other surfaces. The technique appears in carvings, tools, ceremonial objects, and jewelry, with patterns that often reflect stories, symbols, and connections to the land.
INLET: The west coast of Canada is one of the major fjord coastlines of the world, hosting about 150 inlets. The remote and rugged coastline of British Columbia is indented with stunning inlets that cut deep into the Coast Mountains of the BC mainland north of Vancouver. Inlets can be found across the country from coast to coast to coast!
ISLES: Happy St. Patrick's Day from O'Canuckle! Canada is home to many isles with strong Irish heritage! Newfoundland is often called "the most Irish place outside of Ireland," with its distinct dialect, music, and place names reflecting its strong ties to the Emerald Isle. Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton Island also saw Irish settlers shape their communities, contributing to lively traditions of storytelling, music, and St. Patrick's Day celebrations. From coast to coast, Canadians proudly honour their Irish heritage - Sláinte!
ISLET: Today is [World Diabetes Day](https://worlddiabetesday.org/)! Celebrated annually on November 14th, the day marks the birthday of Canadian medical scientist Frederick Banting who, along with Charles Best, first conceived the idea which led to the discovery of insulin in 1922. Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by beta cells of the pancreatic islets. It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and protein by promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into liver, fat and skeletal muscle cells.
JETON: Jetons are small tokens once used for counting and calculations long before modern calculators existed. Today, examples of jetons are part of the national currency collection at the [Bank of Canada Museum](https://www.bankofcanadamuseum.ca/collection/name/view/10/32/74/jeton), highlighting early tools connected to money and commerce. They remind us that even simple objects played an important role in the history of finance in Canada and beyond.
JUNIOR: This year marks the 50th edition of the [IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey Championships](https://www.iihf.com/en/events/2026/wm20), a tournament where the world’s top under-20 players showcase their skills. Canada has long been a powerhouse, winning 20 gold medals and 35 total medals over the decades, more than any other nation. From thrilling goals to unforgettable victories, the tournament celebrates the talent and pride of Canadian hockey’s next generation.
KETCH: A ketch is a two-masted sailboat whose mainmast is taller than the mizzen mast, and whose mizzen mast is stepped forward of the rudder post. HMCS Oriole is the sail training vessel of the Royal Canadian Navy based at CFB Halifax in Halifax, Nova Scotia. She is a sailing ketch, currently the oldest commissioned vessel in the Royal Canadian Navy, and also the longest serving commissioned ship. Oriole celebrated her 100th anniversary in 2021 by making a series of port visits in Atlantic Canada.
KINGS: Today is [Commonwealth Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/commonwealth-day.html)! The 56 member countries of the Commonwealth, including Canada, celebrate Commonwealth Day every year on the second Monday in March. It is a day of observance by more than 2 billion citizens of their common bonds and the contribution of the Commonwealth to the creation of a harmonious global environment. Canada has been a monarchy for centuries - first under the kings of France in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, then under the British Crown in the 18th and 19th centuries, and now as a kingdom in her own right.
KUBIE: A regional specialty from Alberta, the kubie burger is a type of hamburger made from Ukrainian garlic sausage called "kubie" that is pressed and put into a bun. The name comes from kovbasa, which means sausage in Ukrainian. The burger is typically accompanied by fried onions, creamy cheese spreads, caraway bacon sauerkraut, or cheddar cheese and can be found in restaurants, diners, and burger shacks throughout Alberta.
LASER: Canadians Bruce Kirby and Ian Bruce invented the iconic Laser sailboat. The Laser became one of the world's most popular racing sailboats. It became so popular that the Olympic committee added the Laser as an Olympic-class boat for men in 1996 and women in 2008. The Laser’s enduring popularity, though, comes from the thousands of recreational sailors who experience the pure pleasure of single-handing a Laser on a breezy day.
LATCH: Practised by many Indigenous nations along the Northwest Coast of Canada, the potlatch is a ceremonial gathering rooted in generosity, storytelling, music, and the sharing of wealth. Traditionally held to mark major life events like births, weddings, name-giving, and mourning, potlatches are also occasions to reaffirm community ties, pass down ancestral knowledge, and honour cultural laws. Though banned by the Canadian government from 1884 to 1951, potlatches endured and were carried forward with strength and spirit. Today, they continue as powerful expressions of identity, resilience, and cultural pride.
LATTE: September 29th was National Coffee Day! Did you know that lattes are one of the most popular coffee beverages in Canada? In fact, Canadians drink over 1.5 billion cups of coffee annually, with lattes being a go-to choice at many coffee shops. Approximately 7 in 10 Canadians drink coffee daily, making it the most popular beverage in Canada. Whether you prefer it hot or iced, the latte has firmly secured its place in Canada's coffee culture, keeping Canadians caffeinated coast to coast!
LEDGE: [Balancing Rock](https://www.novascotia.com/see-do/attractions/balancing-rock/2582) in Nova Scotia is a famous volcanic rock balanced precariously on a ledge above the waves of St. Mary's Bay. Called "Nature's Time Post", the Balancing Rock is a narrow vertical column of basalt, balanced on its tip that appears to defy gravity. It is estimated to weigh over 20 tonnes and stands 9 metres (20 feet) tall. It's the most photographed of Long Island's striking basalt formations.
LEGAL: [Street Legal](https://gem.cbc.ca/street-legal) is a Canadian legal drama television series, which aired on CBC Television from 1987 to 1994. Street Legal was the longest-running one-hour scripted drama in the history of Canadian television, holding the record for twenty years before being surpassed by Heartland in 2015.
LEGIT: Totally Legit Productions is a Canadian entertainment company known for creating live theatre experiences filled with music, comedy, and storytelling. Their popular production [Oh Canada Eh?! Dinner Musical](https://www.ohcanadaeh.com/) celebrates all things Canadiana with a lively mix of familiar songs, humour, and traditions, bringing audiences together for a fun-filled celebration of what makes Canada special.
LLAMA: Did you know that llamas are not only found in South America but also have a growing presence in Canada? Llamas have been introduced to Canadian farms and are primarily used for their wool, as pack animals, and in eco-friendly agricultural practices. These gentle and intelligent creatures are well-suited to the Canadian climate and can be found on farms across the country, particularly in British Columbia and Ontario. Additionally, llamas have become popular attractions at petting zoos and educational farms, where visitors can learn about their unique characteristics and benefits.
LOCAL: According to a new report by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, over nine in ten Canadians (92%) said they love having small businesses in their community, but only 13% do most of their shopping locally. Small businesses are the cornerstones of our communities and foster a strong sense of community. We encourage Canadians to prioritize shopping local not just during the holiday season, but all year long! #ShopLocal
LOGIC: Happy Star Trek Day! In the Star Trek universe, Vulcans are an extraterrestrial humanoid species known as logical beings who have removed emotions from their daily lives. The official Star Trek Capital of Canada is Vulcan, Alberta. The town even has a prominent display of a Starship Enterprise statue. Live long and prosper! 🖖
LOWER: The Province of Lower Canada was a British colony on the lower Saint Lawrence River and the shores of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence (1791-1841). It covered the southern portion of the current Province of Quebec and the Labrador region of the current Province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
LUNAR: Happy Lunar New Year! The Lunar New Year is an event celebrated by millions of people across the world on the first new moon of their calendar. It marks the beginning of the new year based on the lunar calendar or lunisolar calendar. It is one of the largest celebrations for Canada's Chinese population, and it is also celebrated by Canadians from Vietnam, Korea and Southeast Asia, among others.
MACAW: Macaws bring a splash of colour to the tropical rainforest at [Montréal’s Biodôme](https://espacepourlavie.ca/), where they live among lush plants and other animals from the Americas. The Biodôme itself has an equally colourful history: it was originally built as the velodrome for the 1976 Montréal Olympics before being transformed into an immersive showcase of five American ecosystems. When it opened in 1992, its ecosystem-based approach was considered a world first.
MAGIC: The [International Brotherhood of Magicians](https://www.magician.org/) (I.B.M.) is an organization for both professional and amateur close-up and stage magicians, with approximately 15,000 members worldwide. It was founded in Winnipeg, Manitoba in 1922, and is now the largest organization of magicians in the world. Winnipeg was also home to one of Canada's most famous magicians, Doug Henning, who had a storied career around the world. He retired in the mid-1980s, selling some of his most famous illusions to another famous magician, David Copperfield.
MANIA: Canada experienced "Trudeaumania" in the late 1960s and early 1970s, a wave of excitement sparked by Pierre Trudeau, the charismatic leader of the Liberal Party. With his progressive policies, youthful energy, and charm, Trudeau became a symbol of change and modernity during a transformative period in Canadian history. His rise to power as Prime Minister in 1968 captivated Canadians from coast to coast. "Trudeaumania" saw fans attending packed rallies, sporting Trudeau-inspired fashion, and collecting buttons and memorabilia. This phenomenon left a lasting impact on Canadian politics and culture, marking a unique and spirited chapter in the nation's political history.
MANIC: Quebec is home to [Manic‑5](https://www.hydroquebec.com/facility-tours/tours-general-public/daniel-johnson-manic-5-cote-nord.html), the world’s largest multiple‑arch‑and‑buttress dam, spanning the Manicouagan River. Since its completion in 1970, it has generated hydroelectric power for Quebec and beyond, making it a cornerstone of the province’s clean energy system. Now known as the Daniel‑Johnson Dam, the steady hum of this engineering marvel is a reminder of the massive, reliable infrastructure that keeps Canada running.
MANOR: [Escape Manor](https://www.escapemanor.com/) is known for its interactive and immersive escape rooms in Ottawa, but on September 10, 2017, they organized the world's largest scavenger hunt consisting of 2,732 people! Participants took part in the scavenger hunt in celebration of Canada's 150th anniversary and attempted to complete as many of the 150 tasks as they could throughout the city of Ottawa. Canada now holds the Guinness World Record for the largest scavenger hunt thanks to Escape Manor!
MEATY: If you are looking for hearty comfort food, look no further than French Canadian Tourtière, a meaty, flavourful pie that is typically enjoyed around the holidays (but is also enjoyed all year long). The tourtiere is a traditional Quebecois spiced meat pie, and the ground or chopped filling usually includes pork and is sometimes mixed with other meats, including local game, such as rabbit, pheasant, or moose. Tourtière is the quintessential Canadian comfort food that has a worldwide appeal!
MEDIC: Jennie Trout became Canada’s first licensed female physician in 1875 when she received her medical licence from the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario. As a trailblazing medic, she challenged 19th-century norms and opened doors for women in medicine. Trout went on to establish a successful practice in Toronto, inspiring countless women to follow in her footsteps. Her legacy remains a milestone in Canadian healthcare history.
METRO: Metro systems help move millions of Canadians every day, with rapid transit networks operating in cities like Toronto, Montréal, Vancouver, and Edmonton. [Canada’s first true metro](https://www.stm.info/en/info/networks/metro) opened in Montréal in 1966, designed with rubber-tired trains to allow for quieter rides and steeper grades. Even during heavy snowfall, these systems are built to keep commuters moving and cities connected year-round.
MINER: Happy National Mining Week! Canada has a rich history of mining, with numerous communities across the country built on the back of the mining industry. One such community is [Estevan, Saskatchewan](https://estevan.ca/), known for its coal mining heritage and the iconic character 'Lignite Louie.' Lignite Louie, a fictional character created by the local mining industry, symbolizes the hardworking spirit and resilience of the miners who toiled underground to extract lignite coal, a type of low-grade coal found in the region. Estevan's coal mines played a vital role in powering Saskatchewan's economy and providing employment opportunities for generations of miners and their families. The next time you hear about a miner in Canada, remember the hardworking men and women who helped build the nation's mining industry and shaped the communities we know today.
MISTY: Niagara Falls is a misty wonder on both sides of the border! While the Maid of the Mist is a historic boat tour in the United States, Canada’s [Niagara City Cruises](https://www.cityexperiences.com/niagara-ca/city-cruises/niagara/) lets visitors experience the spray up close and feel the power of this natural marvel. This iconic ride has thrilled generations, offering an unforgettable view of one of Canada’s most famous landmarks. It’s a truly misty adventure you won’t forget!
MODEM: Canadian inventor and electrical engineer, Dr. Brent Townshend, created a core concept in 1996 that served as the basis for what is known as the 56K bit/sec modem, a groundbreaking technology at the time that allowed for data transfer between two computers at high speeds over standard analog dial-up phone line connections. 56K doesn't seem like much these days, but back in the mid-90s, it was a big step forward in Internet technology!
MOTOR: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! The 2023 Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix is on today in Montréal! The F1 Canadian Grand Prix (F1 Grand Prix du Canada) is an annual motor racing event that has been held in Montréal since 1978. Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, the track on which the motor race is run, is located on Île Notre-Dame at Parc Jean-Drapeau, right in the heart of the majestic Saint Lawrence River. The event is synonymous with festivities and the start of Montréal's summer season. Start your engines!
MOULT: Canada's wild bird population goes through moulting periods every year, shedding and replacing old feathers to stay fit for migration and harsh weather. This natural process helps species like Canada geese and snowy owls prepare for long, cold winters and flights south. While moulting can leave birds a bit bedraggled, it’s vital for their survival - keeping them warm, agile, and able to blend into their environment. So if you spot some scruffy feathers during a Canadian autumn hike, it might just be a bird getting ready for winter!
MOUND: The Kay-Nah-Chi-Wah-Nung Historical Centre, or Manitou Mounds, is Canada's premier concentration of ancient burial mounds. Manitou Mounds National Historic Site, as it was once called, is a vast network of 30 village sites and 15 ancient burial mounds constructed from approximately 5000 BP during the Archaic Period, to 360 BP. It is one of the "most significant centres of early habitation and ceremonial burial in Canada."
MOUSE: Toopy and Binoo is an animated series based on the popular French Canadian book series created by Dominique Jolin that features Toopy the mouse and his best friend Binoo the cat. A total of 175 episodes were produced overall. The show has been broadcast in over 179 countries and dubbed into 30 languages, and a film adaptation was released on August 11, 2023 in theatres across Canada.
MURAL: [The world's tallest mural](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/graffiti-calgary-daim-peter-oliver-beltline-bump-alberta-1.6509542) can be found in downtown Calgary, Alberta! It was completed in the summer of 2022 by internationally renowned graffiti artist Mirko Reisser (known as DAIM) and stands 95 metres high on the side of a building across the train tracks from the Calgary Tower. It took 130 litres of paint primer, 207 litres of base coat paint and 543 cans of spray paint.
NAMES: In 1995, Brent Peterson & Margot Newton, an expectant Toronto couple, combed through thousands of baby names trying to agree on just one. Their debate inspired them to invent [Namesake](https://www.namesakegame.com/), a homegrown Canadian board game where players pair up famous people who share the same first name. Thirty years later, Namesake has been reborn as a free daily web puzzle. Try it for yourself at [namesakegame.com](https://www.namesakegame.com/)!
NICKEL: Canada has a long history with nickel, so much so that our five-cent coin earned its name from the metal! The town of Sudbury, Ontario became one of the world’s leading sources of nickel after a massive deposit was discovered in the late 1800s—thanks to a meteor strike over 1.8 billion years ago! To celebrate this mining heritage, Sudbury is home to the [Big Nickel](https://www.sciencenorth.ca/dynamic-earth), a 9-metre-tall replica of a 1951 Canadian nickel. It’s one of Canada’s most iconic roadside attractions!
NIGHT: Hockey Night in Canada (HNIC) is a weekly Saturday night broadcast of NHL games. It has been a staple in Canadian homes since the first radio broadcast in 1931. HNIC began airing on Saturday nights on CBC Television in 1952. It is Canada’s longest-running television program and the Guinness World Record holder as the longest-running TV sports program. Instant replay even made its world debut on a 1955 Hockey Night in Canada broadcast.
NINTH: Did you know that the border between Canada and the United States along the 49th parallel is the longest undefended international boundary in the world? Stretching over 8,891 kilometres, the 49th parallel serves as the dividing line between the two countries for much of their shared border. The bi-national International Boundary Commission deals with matters relating to marking and maintaining the boundary, and the International Joint Commission deals with issues concerning boundary waters.
NOBLE: Today, Canada marks the Coronation of its new monarch, His Majesty King Charles III, beginning a new chapter in our country's history. In recognition of the RCMP's 150th anniversary and the Coronation, the King was officially presented with RCMP Musical Ride horse "Noble". The King has shared a personal connection to the RCMP as their Honorary Commissioner since 2012, and on Friday he was officially appointed Commissioner-in-Chief of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
NORTH: One of Canada's most famous nicknames is the Great White North.
ODEON: [Cineplex Odeon](https://www.cineplex.com/) is one of Canada’s most iconic movie theatre chains, known for bringing the big-screen experience to audiences from coast to coast. Cineplex began in 1979 at Toronto’s Eaton Centre, while Odeon Theatres had been operating in Canada since the 1940s. The two merged in 1984 to form Cineplex Odeon, where Canadians have enjoyed everything from Hollywood hits to homegrown productions ever since.
OPTIC: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, letting information travel vast distances at incredible speeds. In Canada, optic-based networks expand internet access to rural, remote, and northern communities, connecting them to essential services. As more fibre reaches farther corners of the country, optical technology continues to play a quiet but powerful role in helping Canadians stay connected, no matter where they live.
ORDER: The Order of Canada is how our country honours people who make extraordinary contributions to the nation.
OTTER: Canada is home to both river otters and sea otters. While river otters can be found in every province and territory, sea otters are mainly found on Canada's west coast. Scientists consider the sea otter to be a keystone species - one that modifies and creates its habitat. When it was gone from Canadian waters, kelp forests declined because urchins and other animals that eat seaweed weren't controlled by the otter preying on them. With the return of the otter, kelp forests are in much better shape. This is important because healthy kelp forests provide habitat to fish and reduce coastal erosion by slowing water currents. Sea otters are also of some importance to West Coast Indigenous Peoples - they are depicted in their art and featured in their stories.
OUTER: The vastness of outer space is now a little more Canadian! As the [Artemis II](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/missions/artemis-ii/mission.asp) crew completes its historic lunar flyby mission, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen is aboard the Orion spacecraft, travelling over 400,000 kilometres from Earth. Hansen is the first Canadian to journey this far into outer space, taking part in humanity’s first trip around the Moon in over half a century.
OWLET: An owlet is a young or baby owl, and in Canada, they can be found in forests from coast to coast! One common Canadian species, the Great Horned Owl, raises owlets that leave the nest early – long before they can fly. These brave little “branchers” hop from limb to limb, practising balance and strength while their parents continue to feed and protect them in the wild Canadian woods.
PANDA: The Panda Game is an annual Canadian football game between the two OUA football teams in Ottawa, Ontario: the University of Ottawa Gee-Gees and Carleton University Ravens. It is the most significant rivalry in Canadian university football and is a long-running tradition which has ignited school spirit since 1955. Its name is derived from Pedro the Panda, the trophy presented to the winner each year. The 2023 edition of the Panda Game marked the 54th game in the storied series, with uOttawa holding an all-time record of 37-17.
PANKO: Panko breadcrumbs have become a popular ingredient in Canadian kitchens, especially for creating a light and crispy coating on fish. Atlantic cod and haddock, long associated with Canada’s East Coast fishing communities, are often paired with panko to create delicious seafood dishes that bring together traditional flavours and modern cooking styles.
PAPAL: The word papal refers to the pope, the leader of the Catholic Church. Following the recent passing of Pope Francis, many Canadians are reflecting on his 2022 papal visit to Canada – a "pilgrimage of penance" during which he delivered a historic apology for the Catholic Church's role in residential schools. His words at Maskwacîs, Alberta marked a significant moment in the ongoing journey of truth and reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples.
PARRY: In fencing, a parry is a defensive move used to block an opponent’s attack – an essential skill in a sport where speed and precision are everything. In Canada, fencing has been gaining momentum on the world stage, highlighted by [Eleanor Harvey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/eleanor-harvey/)'s historic bronze medal in women’s foil at the Paris 2024 Olympics, marking the country’s first-ever Olympic podium in the sport.
PARTY: HAPPY CANADA DAY! It's Canada's 156th birthday - the biggest party of the year! We hope everyone is celebrating this great nation at a Canada Day party with friends & family.
PATIO: Happy Victoria Day! Today is a federal Canadian public holiday celebrated annually on the last Monday preceding May 25 to honour Queen Victoria. The holiday has been observed in Canada since at least 1845, originally on Victoria's natural birthday, May 24. Today also marks the unofficial start to the summer season in Canada, and along with the warmer weather comes patio season! However you celebrate this long weekend, we hope you get to enjoy some beautiful weather on a patio and support local businesses!
PEASE: Pease pudding, also known as pease porridge, is a traditional dish in Newfoundland made from split yellow peas that are boiled and mashed to create a creamy, savoury side dish. In Newfoundland, it's a staple accompaniment to Jiggs' dinner, a traditional boiled dinner that includes salted beef, root vegetables, and cabbage. This hearty meal has its roots in the British Isles but has been embraced and adapted by Newfoundlanders, reflecting the island's rich culinary heritage and its connection to British and Irish settlers. Pease pudding showcases the comfort and warmth of Newfoundland cuisine.
PECAN: Pecans bring a rich, nutty flavour to Canadian holiday baking, starring in festive favourites like pecan pies, spiced cookies, and butter tarts. A staple on Christmas tables, these versatile nuts add warmth, crunch, and a touch of sweet tradition to seasonal celebrations across the country.
PEDAL: Pedal power takes over the streets of Ottawa each spring during the [CN Cycle for CHEO](https://cncycle.cheofoundation.com/). Held this year on Sunday, May 3, the event invites thousands of participants of all ages and skill levels to pedal, walk, or roll along scenic, car-free routes in support of the CHEO Foundation. Since its launch, the event has raised millions of dollars to help deliver life-saving care for children and youth across eastern Ontario.
PEKAN: The word pekan comes from the Algonquian name for the fisher, a clever and elusive member of the weasel family found throughout Canada's forests. Despite its name, the pekan doesn't fish - instead, it's one of the few predators that can take down a porcupine! Known for its dark fur and tree-climbing skills, the pekan plays an important role in keeping forest ecosystems balanced. Its name lives on in places like the Pekan Trail in Quebec, showing how Indigenous languages continue to shape the map of Canada.
PELTS: Beaver pelts were an integral part of the early Canadian fur trade economy. The fur trade began in the 1600s in what is now Canada. It continued for more than 250 years. Beaver pelts were among the most sought-after furs due to the popularity of beaver top hats in Europe at the time. While the hunting of beavers was only a small part of life for Indigenous peoples before Europeans came, it soon became the predominant activity in some territories.
PERCH: In Canada, 16 species of perch fish occur, including the yellow perch, the walleye and the sauger. The Canadian waters of Lake Erie are well known for producing monster jumbo perch.
PETTY: Petty Harbour-Maddox Cove is a picturesque fishing village located on the eastern shore of Newfoundland and Labrador, just south of St. John's. This charming community is known for its colourful row houses, stunning coastal views, and rich maritime history. Petty Harbour is not only a haven for fishermen but also a popular spot for tourists seeking to experience Newfoundland's natural beauty and vibrant culture. The village has been featured in various films and television shows, showcasing its stunning landscapes and traditional fishing practices.
PHOTO: Yousuf Karsh was a Canadian photographer known for his portraits of notable individuals. He has been described as one of the greatest portrait photographers of the 20th century. Read more about Karsh at karsh.org.
PIKAS: Did you know that pikas, small rabbit-like mammals, are native to Canada's western mountain regions? Found in the alpine areas of British Columbia, Alberta, and the Yukon, these adorable creatures are expert rock climbers, making their homes in boulder fields. Pikas are known for their distinctive "bark" sound and for gathering and storing plants in large haypiles to prepare for the winter months. Despite their cute appearance, pikas are resilient survivors in the harsh, high-altitude environments of the Canadian Rockies!
PINGO: Pingos are impressive ice-cored hills found in the Arctic and Subarctic. "Pingo" is Inuvialuit for small hill. The Mackenzie Delta in the Northwest Territories has the highest concentration of pingos on Earth, approximately 1,350 of them. Pingos can be as big as a football stadium, up to 70 metres tall, with a circumference exceeding half a kilometre.
PINOT: Pinot grapes have found a home in Canada’s wine regions, including British Columbia’s Okanagan Valley and Ontario’s Niagara Peninsula. Varieties like Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris have helped Canadian winemakers showcase the country’s unique climates and growing conditions.
PIPER: Rowdy Roddy Piper was one of Canada’s most iconic professional wrestlers. Born in Saskatchewan, he became a global superstar known for his sharp wit, fearless persona, and unforgettable catchphrases. Piper famously entered the ring wearing his signature kilt, accompanied by bagpipe music, a nod to his Scottish heritage. He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2005 and remains a legend of sports entertainment.
PITON: Canada is home to some of the world's most breathtaking rock climbing destinations! The Canadian Rockies, located in Alberta and British Columbia, boast towering peaks, sheer rock faces, and challenging routes that attract climbers from around the globe. One iconic feature of rock climbing in Canada is the use of pitons, metal spikes hammered into cracks and crevices to secure ropes and protect climbers. While pitons have become less common due to environmental concerns and advances in climbing equipment, they played a significant role in the history of Canadian climbing.
PIXEL: [IMAX](https://www.imax.com/en/ca), the groundbreaking cinematic format known for its jaw-dropping visuals, was proudly invented in Canada! Developed by Graeme Ferguson and his team in the 1960s, IMAX changed the movie experience forever – first with giant film reels, and now with advanced digital projection powered by millions of pixels. Each pixel helps create the stunning clarity and immersive scale that make IMAX unlike anything else. From its roots at home to theatres around the globe, it’s a pixel-powered breakthrough showcasing Canadian innovation!
PODGE: Hodge podge is a favourite vegetable stew from Nova Scotia. Hodge podge originally comes from Acadians living in Nova Scotia who would harvest their vegetables at the height of summer from their garden and immediately make them into a soup using butter and cream. Hodge podge is basic, soul warming food, that celebrates fresh produce - it's a true East Coast classic!
POINT: Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is an important rest stop for migrating birds. [Point Pelee National Park](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/on/pelee) is Canada's second smallest but most ecologically diverse national park, and is home to more than 390 bird species and 70 species of trees, some of which are species at risk.
POLAR: Canada is home to about 16,000 polar bears, which is approximately two-thirds of the world's total estimated population.
POTASH: Potash is a key ingredient in fertilizer—and Canada is the world’s largest producer! Mined primarily in Saskatchewan, potash helps crops grow by boosting potassium in soil, making it vital to global food production. With deep roots in Canada’s Prairie economy, this pinkish mineral is quietly feeding the world, one field at a time.
PRAIRIE: The Prairie provinces—Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta—are home to some of Canada’s most iconic landscapes: endless skies, golden wheat fields, and gently rolling grasslands. These lands hold deep cultural and ecological importance, rooted in Métis and Indigenous histories and home to species like the burrowing owl and bison. They’re also at the heart of Canadian agriculture, producing much of the country’s grain, canola, and pulses. It’s a region where farming traditions, wide-open space, and natural beauty come together under one big prairie sky.
PRIDE: Since 2016, the month of June has been declared Pride Month in Canada to celebrate the LGBTQ2+ community.
PRIME: The Prime Minister (PM) is the head of the federal government in Canada. It is the most powerful position in Canadian politics. While the Queen may be Canada's head of state, and the Governor General the Queen's representative, it's the Prime Minister who is known as the nation's head of government.
PRINT: Happy Labour Day! Labour Day has been marked as a statutory public holiday in Canada on the first Monday in September since 1894. However, the origins of Labour Day in Canada can be traced back to numerous local demonstrations and celebrations in earlier decades. Such events assumed political significance in 1872, when an April labour demonstration in Toronto, in support of the printers of the Toronto Typographical Union on strike for a nine-hour day, led directly to the enactment of the Trade Unions Act, a law that confirmed the legality of unions. The Printers' Strike of 1872, part of the Nine Hour Movement, was a key moment in Canadian labour history and marked the start of a shorter workday.
PRISM: [Prism](https://prism.ca/) (styled as PRiSM) is a Canadian rock band formed in Vancouver in 1977. Their classic line-up consisted of lead singer Ron Tabak, guitarist Lindsay Mitchell, keyboardist John Hall, bassist Allen Harlow and drummer Rocket Norton. They have released a total of eight studio albums, three compilation albums and one live album and they won the Canadian music industry Juno Award for 'Group of the Year' in 1981. A pre-fame Bryan Adams contributed as a songwriter to several early Prism releases.
PRUNE: Vinarterta is a classic holiday cake that has become more common in Canada than Iceland, where it is believed to have originated. The beautiful celebration cake traditionally consists of multiple uniform layers of biscuits sandwiched together with a homemade prune jam that’s loaded with wintry spices. The recipe was brought to Manitoba by Icelandic immigrants to Canada, many of whom initially settled at New Iceland on the west shore of Lake Winnipeg. Manitoba’s Icelandic population has made the vínarterta a staple dessert in the region. If you want to try some authentic Vinarterta, check out [The Icelandic Festival of Manitoba](https://www.icelandicfestival.com/) "Islendingadagurinn" in Gimli, Manitoba which runs from Aug 4-7, 2023!
PURSE: Long before modern handbags, Indigenous artisans across Canada crafted beautiful and functional purses using materials from the land. Caribou hide was carefully prepared for durability and softness, then adorned with intricate glass beadwork introduced through early trade. These handmade purses were not only practical – they often carried deep cultural meaning, with patterns and colours reflecting identity, community, and tradition.
PYLON: Pylons are a common sight across Canada, appearing during construction to guide traffic and keep workers safe – because in this country, everyone knows there are only two seasons: winter and construction! With hockey season underway, 'pylon' is hockey slang for anyone easy to skate around. Whether blocking traffic or getting deked out of their boots, pylons are just part of life in Canada!
QUESO: Queso might be a Tex-Mex favourite, but one of Canada’s go-to spots is homegrown! [Lone Star Texas Grill](https://lonestartexasgrill.com/) opened its first Ottawa location in 1986, serving up warm queso dip, fresh tortilla chips, and sizzling fajitas. Nearly 40 years later, it’s still proudly Canadian-owned – with a Texas twist that’s earned fans from coast to coast.
QUOTA: Fishing quotas play an important role in managing Canada’s marine resources. In 1992, the federal government placed a major moratorium on the Atlantic cod fishery after decades of overfishing led to the collapse of cod stocks, dramatically impacting communities across Newfoundland and Labrador. Since then, strict quotas and management measures have been used to help protect remaining fish populations and support the long-term sustainability of Canada’s fisheries.
RADIO: Canadian inventor Reginald A. Fessenden is best known for his pioneering work developing radio technology, including the foundations of amplitude modulation (AM) radio. On 23 December 1900, he was the first person to send audio (wireless telephony) by means of electromagnetic waves, successfully transmitting speech by radio over a distance of about a 1.6 kilometres.
RANCH: Cattle ranching is the most common type of ranching in Canada, with over 70% of ranches raising beef cattle. Canada is the fourth-largest beef and cattle exporter in the world, with over 60,000 cattle farms and ranches. There are approximately 3.7 million beef cattle in Canada, of which nearly half are in Alberta.
RANGE: Canada is home to some incredible mountain ranges, including the famous Rocky Mountains. The Canadian Rockies house over 50 high mountains whose elevation exceeds the 11,000 ft (3,350 m) mark. The highest peak of this range of mountains is Mount Robson, which stands at 12,972 ft (3,954 m) above mean sea level.
RAVEN: The raven is of high importance to Indigenous Peoples throughout Canada, appearing in myths, legends, art and traditions. It is particularly important to Aboriginal people of the British Columbia coast, where it symbolizes creation, knowledge and prestige. The raven was adopted as the Yukon's official bird in 1985.
REBAR: Rebar (short for "reinforcing bar") is a key material in construction, providing strength and durability to concrete structures. Canada has a strong steel industry, with major production hubs in Ontario, Quebec, and Alberta supplying high-quality rebar for bridges, buildings, and infrastructure projects across the country. Many Canadian steel mills, such as those in Hamilton, Ontario (nicknamed "Steeltown") manufacture rebar using recycled steel, making it both strong and sustainable! So whether it's a towering skyscraper or a sturdy hockey arena, Canadian-made rebar helps build the backbone of our nation!
REELS: Today is [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)! Canada has a rich film history full of memorable stories and incredible talent - both in front of and behind the camera. Before digital editing, movies were physically cut and spliced on film reels, which became a lasting symbol of the film industry. Today, Canadian filmmakers continue to spin powerful stories on screens big and small. So grab some popcorn and press play on a Canadian classic to celebrate the creativity and talent of Canadian filmmakers!
REIGN: The reign of Canada's new monarch, King Charles III, began when Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8. Queen Elizabeth II was Canada's monarch for over 70 years, making her the longest reigning monarch in Commonwealth history.
RELAY: Canada has a proud history of excelling in relay events across multiple sports at the Olympics. Our swimmers have made waves with medal-winning performances, like the women's 4x100m freestyle relay team winning bronze and the women's 4x100m medley relay team winning silver at Tokyo 2020. On the ice, our speed skating teams have brought home numerous medals in the relay events, with the men's 5000m relay team claiming gold at PyeongChang 2018. On the track, Canada's 4x100m men's relay team sprinted to gold in Atlanta 1996, a historic moment anchored by the legendary [Donovan Bailey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/donovan-bailey/). These successes showcase Canada's strength, teamwork, and spirit in relay competitions on the world stage!
RESET: For many Canadians, spring brings more than warmer weather – it’s the season for a full household reset. From washing windows and airing out rooms to clearing garages and tackling winter clutter, spring cleaning has long been a tradition across Canada. After months spent indoors during the colder seasons, many families use this time of year to refresh their homes, routines, and outlook for the months ahead.
RHINO: Did you know Canada once had a political party called the [Rhinoceros Party of Canada](https://www.partyrhino.ca/)? Founded in 1963, it became famous for its satirical and humorous platform. The party proposed outrageous policies like repealing the law of gravity and banning lousy Canadian winters. While they never gained significant political power, the party remains a quirky part of Canadian political history, known for mocking traditional politics and using humour to encourage people to think about the system in a new way.
RIDER: [Canadian equestrian](https://equestrian.ca/) riders have shone brightly on the world stage in both dressage and eventing! [Ian Millar](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/ian-millar/), affectionately known as "Captain Canada," has competed in a record 10 Olympic Games, winning a team silver medal in show jumping at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In dressage, Canada brought home a bronze medal in team dressage from the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Canada’s equestrian success continues to inspire and showcase the dedication and talent of its riders.
RIDGE: The Battle of Vimy Ridge, during the First World War, is Canada's most celebrated military victory – an often mythologized symbol of the birth of Canadian national pride and awareness.
ROBIN: The return of the robin is a sure sign of Spring in Canada! American Robins begin to arrive at their breeding grounds in southern areas of Canada in March each year. Few birds are as familiar to the Canadian public as the robin. Its plumage is easily recognizable, and it is one of the first birds to sing in the morning and one of the last to be heard at night.
ROPER: A roper is a person who uses a lasso to catch an animal, especially in a rodeo. The Calgary Stampede features the best riders, racers and ropers each year!
ROUND: On National Donut Day, Canadians celebrate the sweet, round treat found in bakeries and coffee shops across the country. From classic glazed rings to filled and frosted varieties, donuts are a popular indulgence enjoyed with coffee or hot chocolate. Canada is also among the highest donut-consuming countries in the world, with Canadians enjoying roughly a billion donuts each year. Their familiar round shape is part of what makes them so iconic and instantly recognizable.
ROUSE: "The Rouse" is a bugle call most often associated with the military in Commonwealth countries. It is commonly played following "Last Post" at military services. "The Rouse" was traditionally played following "Reveille", which was a bugle call played in the morning to wake soldiers up.
ROUTE: Today is the 2023 Terry Fox Run! The event is a classic Canadian tradition every Fall with communities and runners across the country coming together to fundraise for cancer research. It is the world's largest one-day fundraiser for cancer research. Terry Fox's route across Canada for his Marathon of Hope started in St. John's, Newfoundland & Labrador and ended early in Thunder Bay, Ontario, but if you stretch the total distance he ran (5,373 km) into a straight line, his route reaches all the way to Vancouver Island's west coast. You can donate to the [Terry Fox Foundation](https://terryfox.org/) in honour of Terry at [terryfox.org](https://terryfox.org/).
ROWAN: The rowan tree, also known as mountain ash, is one of Canada’s most widespread native trees, found from Newfoundland to British Columbia. In autumn, its bright red berry clusters become an important food source for migrating birds such as cedar waxwings, robins, and pine grosbeaks. In Atlantic Canada, Scottish settlers often planted rowans near their homes, carrying with them a Highland tradition that believed the trees brought protection and good fortune. The berries have also been used in Maritime kitchens for generations, turned into jams, jellies, and even rowan wine.
RUGBY: Buoyed by its inclusion in the 2016 Olympic Games, Rugby is one of the fastest growing team sports in Canada, particularly in youth and women.
RULER: Happy [Victoria Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/victoria-day.html)! Celebrated on the last Monday before May 25, the day honours Queen Victoria, the longest-reigning monarch in British history at the time. Known as the 'Mother of Confederation,' her rule from 1837 to 1901 helped shape the modern Canadian nation. As Canada's first monarch after Confederation, her leadership paved the way for a future where Canada would become a self-governing dominion within the British Empire.
RUSTY: Rusty was the cheerful puppet rooster on The Friendly Giant, a classic Canadian children’s television show that aired from 1958 to 1985. Voiced and puppeteered by Canadian Rod Coneybeare, Rusty lived in a book bag that hung on the castle wall, delighting generations of viewers and becoming a symbol of warmth, friendship, and fun in households across Canada.
SANDY: While Canada is famous for its mountains and forests, it also has some of the world's most beautiful sandy beaches. One of the gems is [Sandbanks Provincial Park](https://www.ontarioparks.ca/park/sandbanks) in Ontario, which features the largest freshwater sandbar and dune system in the world! Another beach lover's paradise is Cavendish Beach in Prince Edward Island, with its red sand and rolling dunes. Alongside Wasaga Beach in Ontario, the longest freshwater beach in the world, these natural beauties offer picturesque sandy getaways for visitors and Canadians alike.
SANTA: HO HO HO! Did you know that Santa Claus is a legal Canadian citizen? Santa was declared a full Canadian citizen in 2008 by Canada’s Immigration Minister and was even issued a Canadian passport in 2013! Of course, Santa also has the most famous postal code in Canada: H0H 0H0. Santa's closest neighbours are the Canadians living in Alert, Nunavut, only 820 kilometres from the North Pole. Merry Christmas, eh?
SAPPY: Maple syrup season is upon us in Canada, and that means that it's time to indulge in the sappy goodness! This sweet springtime tradition is celebrated at Maple Syrup Festivals across the country. Did you know that it takes it takes approximately 40 gallons of sap to produce just one delicious gallon of fresh maple syrup? Be sure to take in the maple season and visit your local sugar shack, where every hour is sappy hour!
SCARF: Winter is officially here! The scarf is an essential item of clothing for the winter season in Canada. It's all about layers if you want to be comfortable in the cold weather, and the scarf is one of the best winter accessories for staying warm. The Kokom (Kokum) Scarf or Ukrainian Scarf are a symbol of relations of the Indigenous peoples supporting Ukrainian settlers that arrived to Canada. These scarves were traded among Indigenous and Ukrainian women. There are many similarities between the two cultures and the scarf today resembles unity and respect for each other.
SCAUP: The scaup is a type of diving duck found in Canada, known for its sleek black-and-white plumage and love for deep-water foraging. There are two main species of scaup in Canada: the Lesser Scaup and the Greater Scaup. They're also known for their incredible migratory journeys, flying thousands of kilometres between breeding grounds in Canada and wintering spots along the coasts of the United States.
SCOUT: For more than 100 years, [Scouts Canada](https://www.scouts.ca/) has brought a world of adventure, outdoor experience, friendship and fun to 17 million Canadian youth. Scouts Canada is the country's leading co-ed youth organization, offering programming for children and youth aged 5-26. Scouts Canada is part of the [World Organization of the Scout Movement WOSM](https://www.scout.org/) which has over 40 million members in 167 National Scout Organizations around the world.
SCUBA: In 1839, the Saint John, New Brunswick duo of of James Elliott and Alexander McAvity patented the "Self-contained Underwater Breathing Apparatus," which we now know as the Scuba tank. The Scuba tank revolutionized underwater exploration, allowing divers to explore the depths of the ocean without the constraints of surface connections. The invention has paved the way for ocean research, deep-sea exploration, and recreational diving. Let's give a big round of applause to the Canadian inventors of the Scuba tank!
SEDGE: In Canada, marshy areas known as sedges are important habitats for wildlife, especially for cranes! The term "sedge" not only refers to grassy wetlands but also to a group of cranes gathering in these lush areas. Canada is home to two species of cranes - the Sandhill Crane and the endangered Whooping Crane. Each fall, Sandhill Cranes flock to Canadian wetlands, where sedges provide the perfect mix of cover and food as they prepare for migration. These crane gatherings are a beautiful sight, showcasing how Canada’s diverse ecosystems support unique wildlife year-round.
SEINE: Seine net fishing has been one of the most important methods used on Canada’s Pacific and Atlantic coasts for generations. A seine net encircles a school of fish such as salmon, herring, or mackerel, then closes like a drawstring purse at the bottom. Commonly used by purse seiners in British Columbia during salmon season, the technique has deep roots in both Indigenous and settler fishing traditions and remains a key part of Canada’s coastal fisheries today.
SERGE: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or “Mounties,” are known for their iconic uniforms that feature the iconic scarlet tunic called a red serge.
SERVE: For more than 100 years, millions of Canadians have proudly served our country in uniform. While the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) are known to put their lives on the line to support international operations, they also fulfill important roles on home soil. They provide national and regional security, serve on search and rescue missions and respond to natural disasters. On this Remembrance Day, we honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice. Lest we forget.
SEWER: [Flin Flon](https://cityofflinflon.ca/), Manitoba is known for its unique above-ground “sewer boxes,” wooden-covered utility structures built because the rocky Canadian Shield made underground installation difficult. In the city’s early development, they also doubled as pedestrian walkways and remain a distinctive part of the local infrastructure today.
SHAFT: Goderich, Ontario is home to the world's largest salt mine! Located beneath Lake Huron, the mine shaft is as deep as the height of the CN Tower. Operating since 1959, the rock salt produced at the Sifto Salt Mine is used to keep citizens in North America safe as they travel through winter snow and ice.
SHAKE: Did you know Canada has an island that literally shakes? Tremble Island, located in British Columbia’s Seymour Inlet, experiences a phenomenon where the ground quivers due to the power of the water currents surrounding it. This inlet has some of the fastest tidal surges in the world, and at peak tides, the force of the water is so intense that it causes the entire island to tremble! Visitors to Tremble Island are in for a unique (and slightly shaky) experience, showcasing the raw power of Canada’s incredible natural landscapes.
SHALE: The Burgess Shale is a fossil-bearing deposit exposed in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia, Canada. Found in Canada's Yoho National Park, it is one of the most important fossil sites in the world! The rocks here preserve not only the usual hard shells of ancient organisms, but also soft skin and tissue, allowing for stunning impressions of the strange creatures of 500 million years ago!
SHAVE: Every Movember,Canadians start the month with a clean shave before growing moustaches to raise awareness for men’s health. The movement began in Australia in 2003 and quickly spread worldwide, with Canada becoming one of the top fundraising countries. Through the power of the mo’, Canadians help support research and programs focused on mental health, prostate cancer, testicular cancer, and suicide prevention. Canuckle co-creators Mark & Jeff are growing their moustaches to support the cause! [Visit our Mo Space and make a donation](https://ca.movember.com/mospace/15437932) for all the dads, brothers, sons, and men in your life.
SHAWL: Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. There are a variety of regional dance styles performed by men, women and children across North America. Women were traditionally required to wear shawls as a sign of proper etiquette when in a dancing arena. The characteristic feature of the women's [Fancy Shawl Dance](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/powwow-dances#WomensFancyShawlDance) - the elaborate shawl - is uniquely decorated by the dancer with distinct ornaments, beadwork and fringes. Though diverse in terms of regalia, footwork and origin stories, powwow dances remain a testament to Indigenous history, heritage and identity.
SHEET: In Canada, curling is more than just a sport - it's a winter tradition! The game is played on a long, narrow stretch of ice called a sheet, where teams slide granite stones toward a target. Canada is home to nearly 1,000 curling clubs and some of the world's best curlers. Today, all eyes are on Kelowna, BC, for the final of the [Montana's Brier](https://www.curling.ca/2025brier/)! The country's top men's teams are battling it out on the sheets for a chance to be crowned Canadian champions. Hurry hard!
SHIRT: Feb 22 is Anti-Bullying Day, also known as [Pink Shirt Day](https://www.pinkshirtday.ca/), where people wear a pink-coloured shirt to stand against bullying. The initiative was started in Canada in 2007 by two Nova Scotia teenagers when a fellow Grade 9 student in Berwick was being teased and bullied for wearing a pink shirt on the first day of school.
SILVER: Canada’s silver rush began near [Cobalt, Ontario](https://cobalt.ca/), in 1903, sparking a mining boom that transformed the small northern community into one of the world’s great silver-producing regions. Cobalt’s mines yielded millions of ounces of silver each year, earning the town the nickname “Silver Capital of Canada.” The rush attracted thousands of prospectors and miners, and the wealth and expertise generated there helped fuel the development of mining across northern Ontario.
SIXTH: June 6th marks the anniversary of D-Day, when Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy during the Second World War in 1944. Known as Operation Overlord, the invasion began on the sixth day of June and became one of the largest amphibious military operations in history. Canadian forces played a major role on Juno Beach, fighting alongside Allied troops in a pivotal moment that helped turn the tide of the war in Europe.
SKIER: Approximately 275 Canadian ski areas see more than 19 million visits per season. Canadian skiers and snowboarders (an estimated number of 2.5 million) are on the slopes and trails an average of 7.5 days per year.
SKIRT: Ribbon skirts represent an important part of the identity and history of Indigenous women and girls. January 4th marked the first [National Ribbon Skirt Day in Canada](https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/canada-marks-national-ribbon-skirt-day-inspired-by-10-year-old-saskatchewan-girl/). Every Jan 4 going forward will be a day where Indigenous women across the country are encouraged to wear ribbon skirts to celebrate their culture, their strength and their connection as women.
SLEEP: For many young people in Canada, a safe place to sleep isn’t guaranteed. [Covenant House](https://covenanthouse.ca/) – the country’s largest agency serving youth who are homeless, trafficked, or at risk – hosts Sleep Out events in cities like Toronto and Vancouver to raise funds and awareness for youth experiencing homelessness. One night outdoors helps provide countless youth with warmth, support, and a safe place to sleep. You can [donate to Covenant House today](https://secure.covenanthouse.ca/page/167256/donate/1) to help make an impact.
SLEET: Sleet is a familiar part of Canadian winters, forming when snowflakes melt into raindrops and then refreeze before hitting the ground. Canada experiences some of the widest temperature swings on Earth, which makes mixed precipitation like sleet especially common in late fall and early spring. In fact, parts of southern Canada can see all four types of precipitation – rain, snow, sleet, and freezing rain – within the same day!
SLICE: In Newfoundland and Labrador, a humble slice of bologna takes on legendary status! Affectionately known as “Newfie steak,” thick slices of this processed meat are pan-fried until crispy and golden brown. Served solo, in sandwiches, or even at community breakfasts, it’s a beloved comfort food with big flavour and even bigger heart. Whether sizzling in a skillet or served on a bun with mustard, it’s a slice of East Coast tradition!
SLIDE: The Frank Slide was a massive rockslide that buried part of the mining town of Frank in the District of Alberta of the North-West Territories (now the province of Alberta) on April 29, 1903. The site of the disaster, which remains nearly unchanged since the slide, is now a popular tourist destination. It has been designated a provincial historic site of Alberta and is home to an interpretive centre that receives over 100,000 visitors annually. Visit [frankslide.ca](https://frankslide.ca) to learn more about Canada's deadliest rockslide.
SLUSH: In Newfoundland and Labrador, it’s not Christmas without slush! This shockingly easy and potent batch cocktail is a holiday must-have in the easterly province and, abandoning all cocktail etiquette, is prepared in a salt beef bucket. Christmas slush is traditionally prepared with amber rum, frozen cans of lemonade and orange juice concentrate, pineapple juice and a whole lot of sugar. Newfoundland Christmas slush encapsulates beloved tradition, a sense of community and holiday hospitality in Newfoundland and Labrador.
SMELT: Fresh smelt are a cold-weather harvest for fishers in Canada. Pan-fried with flour and butter, some rank smelt right up there with lobster and scallops on the tasty-scale. Smelts can be found in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, as well as some freshwater lakes across Canada. Indigenous peoples in Canada native to the Great Lakes regions were both familiar and partially dependent upon smelts as a dietary source of protein and omega fats.
SMOKE: Today is National Indigenous Peoples Day! Smoke is used in different ways by all three Indigenous groups in Canada. Whether it is to smoke fish and meat, to burn sage and tobacco or for sacred ceremonies or celebrations, it is a significant symbol in Indigenous culture.
SNEER: Remember Cyril Sneer from The Raccoons? That pink-nosed villain with a love for money and a signature scowl was part of a classic Canadian cartoon created by Kevin Gillis and produced by Sheldon Wiseman. Set in the Evergreen Forest, the series followed raccoon friends who often found themselves standing up to Cyril's scheming ways - all while promoting messages of friendship, conservation, and doing the right thing. A true gem of Canadian animation!
SNOWY: On February 10, 1999, Tahtsa Lake, British Columbia got hit with 145 cm (4'9") of snow in ONE day!
SOOTY: The Sooty Grouse is a large, forest-dwelling bird found along Canada’s Pacific coast. In Canada, it is primarily found in British Columbia, where it inhabits coastal and interior mountain forests from Vancouver Island to the mainland ranges. These non-migratory birds are best known for their distinctive spring courtship displays.
SPOOR: In Canada, spoor refers to the tracks or signs left by animals in the wild, like deer, moose, wolves, or lynx. From snow-covered forests to muddy riverbanks, following spoor has helped naturalists, trappers, and Indigenous communities study and track wildlife for generations. In the Canadian wilderness, where vast forests and frozen landscapes can make spotting wildlife difficult, spoor provides a hidden map of animal life waiting to be discovered.
SQUAB: A squab is a young pigeon, once raised on Canadian farms as a delicacy for its tender meat. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, squab was served in hotels and dining halls across the country. While today pigeons are more often spotted on city streets and town squares, the word squab offers a glimpse into Canada’s rich farming and culinary traditions.
SQUIB: In the world of film and TV production, a squib is a small, controlled explosion used to simulate bullet hits or sudden impact – often seen in action movies. Canada, particularly Vancouver (a.k.a. Hollywood North) and Toronto, is a global hub for filming, and many productions here rely on Canadian special effects artists to rig squibs for dramatic scenes. If you've watched series like The Boys, Reacher, or even older hits like X-Men, chances are you've seen squib effects made and managed by Canadian crews.
SQUID: The Canadian fishing village of Glover's Harbour, Newfoundland (formerly known as Thimble Tickle) claims to be the "Home of the Giant Squid." It earned this distinction in 1878, when a living giant squid was discovered stranded offshore. Now enshrined in the form of a "life-sized" sculpture, the world's largest squid is the subject of an annual festival, and in 2011, the sculpture was featured on a Canadian postage stamp.
START: In 2025, [Canadian Tire’s Jumpstart program](https://jumpstart.canadiantire.ca/) celebrates 20 years of helping kids across Canada start their journey in sports by removing financial barriers. Since 2005, Jumpstart has provided funding for equipment, registration fees, and transportation so thousands of children can get active, build confidence, and feel part of their communities. Getting a great start in sports helps kids grow stronger – on the field and off.
STATE: Canada's political system is based on that of the United Kingdom. It is a constitutional monarchy, which means that we recognize the Queen or King as the Head of State, while the Prime Minister is the Head of Government. Currently, His Majesty King Charles III is King of Canada and Canada's Head of State. He is the personal embodiment of the Crown in Canada. A state funeral for former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney is being held today in Montreal. Wayne Gretzky will be among the high-profile figures to eulogize the former PM. Mulroney passed away on Feb 29, 2024 at the age of 84. He served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993.
STEEL: Steel plays an extremely important role in the Canadian economy as a whole: in 2019, the Canadian steel industry contributed $4.2 billion to Canada's GDP. According to the Canadian Steel Producers Association, the Canadian steel industry employs, directly and indirectly, more than 120,000 Canadians.
STEIN: Raise a stein to Kitchener-Waterloo [Oktoberfest](https://www.oktoberfest.ca/), one of the largest Bavarian festivals outside Germany! First held in 1969, the annual celebration honours the region’s strong German-Canadian heritage with traditional food, music, dancing and festivities throughout the community. It’s a fitting tradition for Kitchener, a city once known as Berlin before being renamed in 1916.
STERN: Located in Kaslo, British Columbia, the [S.S. Moyie stern wheeler](https://www.klhs.bc.ca/) is the oldest intact passenger steam vessel of its type in the world. The machinery and the steel frames of its hull were built by the Bertram Engine Works of Toronto, shipped west by rail and assembled in Vancouver. Launched at Nelson on 22 October 1898 by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the S.S. Moyie carried passengers and freight on Kootenay Lake for 59 years. It was retired from service in 1957. Rescued and preserved by the people of Kaslo, the "sweetheart of the lake" recalls the role of sternwheelers in the history of western Canada. 2023 marks the 125th birthday celebration of the S.S. Moyie, which was designated a national historic site of Canada in 1958 and reaffirmed in 1983.
STOAT: Stoats, also known as short-tailed weasels or ermines, are widespread across Canada. Found in most regions, they grow a white winter coat for camouflage, slipping through snow and tunnels as fearless hunters of mice, voles, birds, and insects. That same nimble, energetic spirit comes to life in [Tina and Milo](https://www.olympics.com/en/milano-cortina-2026/brand/mascots), the stoat siblings who are mascots for the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics, bringing fun, cheer, and Olympic excitement to athletes and fans alike.
STONY: [Stony Plain](https://www.stonyplain.com/) is a town in the Edmonton Metropolitan Region of Alberta that is situated on the traditional lands of Treaty 6 peoples. Stony Plain is known for its many painted murals representing various periods, events and people throughout the town's history. The town was originally known as Dog Rump Creek. Stony Plain is also home to [Canadian History Ehx](https://canadaehx.com/) podcaster and historian, [Craig Baird](https://x.com/CraigBaird), who explores the good, the bad and the weird of Canada's history. Join Canuckle in wishing Craig a very happy birthday today!
STORE: The local convenience store has been the backbone of Canadian communities for generations. In fact, our convenience store roots can be traced back to Quebec in the 1600s when Samuel de Champlain founded the first store outside of Quebec City. The more than 22,500 stores across Canada act as gathering places in many communities. Those community hubs generate more than $54 billion in sales, employ more than 200,000 Canadians and sell everything from fuel, EV charging, to lottery, energy drinks, bottled water, salty snacks and in Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, beer. Find out more about Canada’s convenience industry from its chief advocate, The Convenience Industry Council of Canada at [convenienceindustry.ca](https://convenienceindustry.ca/).
STOUT: Happy [Canadian Beer Day](https://canadianbeerday.ca/)! During the early period of Canada’s brewing history, heavier ales, porters and stouts were the more popular brews, owing to the traditional preferences of the English, Irish, Welsh and Scottish immigrants who comprised an increasing proportion of Canada’s population following the takeover of New France by Britain in 1763.
STOVE: The stove was the true heart of many early Canadian pioneer homes. Cast-iron wood stoves provided the main source of heat during long, freezing winters while also serving as the primary place for cooking meals, heating water, and gathering as a family. For many settlers, the stove was more than an appliance, it was an essential part of daily life and survival in Canada’s harsh climate.
STRAY: The Parliament Hill cat colony was a clowder of stray cats living on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario, in a cat sanctuary set aside for them. The care of the cats and maintenance of the sanctuary was carried out by volunteers, and the effort was funded by donations. The colony was closed in January 2013 after the remaining cats were adopted into homes.
STYLE: Style in Canada is as diverse as the country itself – from cozy winter layers to cutting-edge couture. Canada’s fashion scene celebrates creativity and identity, with Montréal’s vibrant design houses and [Toronto’s Fashion Week](https://fashionarttoronto.ca/) runways leading the way. Brands like [Canada Goose](https://www.canadagoose.com/ca/en/home-page), [Smythe](https://shopsmythe.com/), and Indigenous-owned labels such as [Lesley Hampton](https://lesleyhampton.com/) and [Section 35](https://www.sectionthirtyfive.com/) show how Canadian style blends function, culture, and artistry – proof that true northern style never goes out of fashion!
SUGAR: Spring is only a few weeks away, and that means it's almost sugar season! Sugar shacks ("cabanes à sucres" in French) are cabins where sap is collected from sugar maple trees and boiled into maple syrup. In 2022, over 72 million litres of maple syrup came out of sugar shacks in Quebec, accounting for over 90% of Canada's domestic production.
SUITE: [Honeymoon Suite](https://honeymoonsuiteband.com/) is a Canadian rock band that was formed in 1981 in Niagara Falls, Ontario. The band's name was inspired by the fact that Niagara Falls is the unofficial honeymoon capital of the world. Honeymoon Suite won the Juno Award for Group of the Year in 1986.
SWEET: Today is National Donut Day in Canada! November 5th is one of two days observed by donut lovers across the nation. The first Friday in June is the other day we celebrate everything about sweet, delicious donuts. That's right...we celebrate TWO National Donut Days in our country! Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! Whether sugar-coated, glazed, or even jelly-filled, the round-shaped treat can make your day all the more sweet!
SYNOD: A synod is a council or assembly in some Christian denominations to discuss and decide on matters of doctrine, administration, and other church affairs. In Canada, faith and religion play a significant role in the country's cultural mosaic. The Anglican and Lutheran churches in Canada often hold synods to guide their spiritual and organizational direction, reflecting their long-standing traditions within the country's diverse religious landscape. Canada’s religious diversity is reflected in the various synods and assemblies held by different Christian communities, contributing to the rich tapestry of beliefs and practices across the nation.
