TANGO: Did you know that Canada has a unique connection to the tango? While the dance originated in Argentina, it's celebrated worldwide, including on International Day of the Tango on December 11th! In Canada, tango thrives through organizations like [PointeTango](https://pointetango.com/), a Canadian dance company that combines traditional tango with ballet, bringing this iconic dance to new audiences. By pushing new boundaries in dance, PointeTango combines the intimacy of Argentine tango with the precision of classical ballet, creating a new dance vocabulary that is both intimate and bold.
TARTS: A butter tart is a delicious pastry tart, which generally consists of butter, sugar, syrup, and egg, filled into a flaky pastry. The earliest published recipe for a butter tart is from Barrie, Ontario dating back to 1900 in the Women's Auxiliary of the Royal Victoria Hospital Cookbook.
TATER: Today is National Potato Day! Did you know that potatoes are grown in every province in Canada? The largest production of taters is in Prince Edward Island, followed by Manitoba, Alberta and New Brunswick. Approximately 64% of potatoes are destined for processing (frozen French fries, potato chips, and other dried products), 24% for fresh table consumption, and 12% for seed. Potatoes are the most valuable vegetable crop in Canada. There are close to 1,000 potato farms across Canada that produce approximately $1.4 billion worth of potatoes each year.
TAXIS: Taxis have played an important role in Canadian urban history since the early 20th century, with cities like Winnipeg and Toronto among the first to introduce motorized taxi services. During World War II, Canadian taxi fleets were repurposed for civil defense – transporting supplies, volunteers, and even serving as emergency vehicles when needed. Today, while rideshares are popular, classic yellow cabs remain a familiar sight in many of Canada’s biggest cities.
TEAMS: Fifty [Canadian Paralympians](https://paralympic.ca/games/milano-cortina-2026/athletes/) are bound for the 2026 Winter Paralympics, which open on March 6! They’ll compete across six sports: para alpine skiing, para biathlon, para cross-country skiing, para ice hockey, para snowboarding, and wheelchair curling. From individual races to medal-contending teams on the ice and snow, they’ll challenge 665 athletes from around the world across 79 medal events. Together, these teams and athletes bring skill, strategy, and teamwork to every course and match, representing the strength and resilience of the Canada Paralympic Team.
TEETH: Did you know the humble zipper owes its "teeth" to Canadian ingenuity? In 1913, while working for the Universal Fastener Company, Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-born inventor who settled in St. Catharines, Ontario, developed the modern zipper we use today. His design - originally called the "Separable Fastener" - featured interlocking metal teeth that made it easy to open and close. Though small, this invention would go on to revolutionize fashion, camping gear, and much more. Next time you zip up, give a nod to Canada's history of clever creations!
TEMPO: The tempo is picking up for women's basketball in Canada! The WNBA is expanding north with the [Toronto Tempo](https://tempo.wnba.com/), the league's first-ever Canadian franchise. Set to debut in 2026, the Tempo will bring top-tier professional women's basketball to Toronto, igniting excitement among fans across the country. The team's ownership group includes tennis legend Serena Williams, who is bringing her influence to the sport. With Canada's strong basketball talent and growing support for the sport, the Tempo are sure to make an impact on the court!
TENOR: [The Tenors](https://www.tenorsmusic.com/) (formerly known as The Canadian Tenors) are a vocal group consisting of Victor Micallef, Clifton Murray, Alberto Urso, and Mark Masri. They sing operatic pop music and have performed on more than 60 international television programs, including the Oprah Winfrey Show and the Emmy Awards. They sang at the 2009 and 2016 Grey Cup, the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, and the 2017 Invictus Games in Toronto, and won a Juno Award in 2013 for Adult Contemporary Album of the Year.
TENTH: Newfoundland and Labrador became Canada’s tenth province on March 31, 1949, following a historic vote to join Confederation. Originally known simply as Newfoundland, the province was officially renamed Newfoundland and Labrador in 2001 to better reflect its mainland territory. From colourful coastal towns to rugged northern landscapes, it’s a uniquely vibrant part of Canada’s story – tenth to join, but first in East Coast charm!
TENTS: Camping is a cherished Canadian tradition, with tents set up each summer in provincial and national parks from coast to coast to coast. From lakeside campgrounds to remote backcountry sites, Canadians head outdoors to paddle, hike, and sleep under the stars. Pitching a tent is one of the simplest ways many people connect with Canada’s vast natural landscapes and seasonal wilderness culture.
TEPEE: The tepee (also commonly spelled tipi or teepee) played a vital role in the lives of many Plains First Nations, including the Blackfoot, Cree, and Nakoda. Its portable design made it ideal for following the buffalo herds, while its ingenious construction kept families comfortable through Prairie summers and winters alike. Today, tepees continue to be raised at powwows, gatherings, and ceremonies across Canada, honouring enduring Indigenous traditions and cultures.
THANK: Today we are celebrating Canuckle #1500! Reaching this milestone was a moment to pause and thank the community that has made 1500 daily puzzles possible. From coast to coast to coast, and around the world, Canuckle has become a shared part of many people’s daily routine – a quick challenge, a few guesses, and a lot of connection along the way. We’re incredibly grateful to everyone who has played, shared, and supported the game since day one. Thank you!
THEIR: [Their Opportunity](https://www.theiropportunity.com/) is a national children's charity in Canada that uses sport and generosity to educate, uplift, and support children facing barriers. Their programs break down obstacles to participation and promote a lifestyle of giving back, empowering youth to grow, belong, and thrive. Their Opportunity is one of the charities supported by the [Sach In Motion](https://sachinmotion.ca/) fund, as Sachin Latti completes his coast-to-coast run in St. John’s, Newfoundland today, raising awareness and support for mental health and community causes.
THIGH: Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario, celebrates [100 years of Homecoming](https://www.queensu.ca/alumni/homecoming) this weekend, and few traditions are more closely tied to the occasion than the [Oil Thigh](https://www.queensu.ca/encyclopedia/o/oil-thigh). Dating back to 1891, the Queen’s song and dance takes its name from the Gaelic words “Oil thigh na Banrighinn” and is still performed by students and alumni at football games, Homecoming and other university celebrations.
THING: [The Nature of Things](https://www.cbc.ca/natureofthings/) is television’s longest-running science series that debuted on CBC on November 6, 1960. It evolved into an hour-long documentary during renowned Canadian scientist and environmental activist David Suzuki’s tenure as host (1979–2023). The groundbreaking program was among the first to present scientific findings on subjects such as HIV/AIDS and climate change. Over the course of more than 60 seasons and over 900 episodes, The Nature of Things has been seen in more than 80 countries. It has received 17 Gemini Awards and seven Canadian Screen Awards.
THIRD: In curling, the third is the player who throws the third pair of stones and helps the skip plan strategy. At the 2026 Winter Olympics, Team Canada’s thirds [Marc Kennedy](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/marc-kennedy/) and [Tracy Fleury](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/tracy-fleury/) play a crucial role in every end, delivering precise shots, calling key plays, and helping their teams chase medals on the world stage. Their decisions on the ice can change the course of an entire match.
THORN: Canada has a deep-rooted love for roses, particularly the hardy Canadian Explorer rose series, developed to withstand cold winters. The [Canadian Rose Society](https://canadianrosesociety.org/), founded in 1946, promotes the appreciation and cultivation of roses across the country. Thorny roses are celebrated at the annual "Festival of Roses" held at Montréal Botanical Garden, which showcases hundreds of beautiful rose varieties. While roses have their thorns, they are a symbol of perseverance and beauty, much like the spirit of Canadian gardeners who cultivate them in challenging climates.
THREE: Happy National Sisters Day! The [Three Sisters](https://www.travelalberta.com/listings/three-sisters-mountains-2010/) are a trio of peaks near Canmore, Alberta. They are known individually as Big Sister (Faith), Middle Sister (Charity) and Little Sister (Hope). These three peaks have a significant role in the town of Canmore, tourism, and hiking in the area and may be the most recognized peaks in the Bow River Valley.
TIDAL: Canada has North America's strongest current! The stretch of the Discovery Passage north of Vancouver Island in Seymour Narrows, British Columbia has some of the strongest tidal currents ever measured with flood speeds of 17 km/h and ebb speeds of 18 km/h. The average width of the narrows is just 750 metres.
TITAN: The [Ottawa Titans](https://www.ottawatitans.com/) are one of three Canadian baseball teams that play in the MLB Partner [Frontier League](https://www.frontierleague.com/). Formed in 1993, it is the oldest currently running independent league in the United States. The Can-Am League merged with the Frontier League in 2019.
TOKEN: When Toronto’s first subway opened on March 30, 1954, commuters used purpose-built [metallic tokens](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/a-look-back-at-the-history-of-ttc-tickets-tokens-and-passes-1.7534088) designed to combat the counterfeiting of paper tickets. TTC tokens became one of the most recognizable objects in Toronto life, handled by generations of riders for nearly seven decades. The last tokens were sold in March 2023, ending a 69-year tradition.
TONNE: Canada officially uses the metric system of measurement, and tonne is the standard spelling of the metric unit for weight. One tonne is equal to 1000kg, or the size of a fully grown bison!
TOONIE: Canada’s two-dollar coin, affectionately called the “toonie,” was introduced in 1996 to replace the $2 bill. It features an adult polar bear, designed by Ontario wildlife artist Brent Townsend, standing on an Arctic ice floe. Its name comes from a playful mix of “two” and “loonie,” the one-dollar coin. In 2002, a giant toonie statue was unveiled in Campbellford, Ontario, honouring one of the country’s most recognizable coins.
TOPAZ: Hidden beneath Canada's rugged landscapes, topaz can be found glimmering across the country, including in Bancroft, Ontario - Canada's 'Mineral Capital' - as well as in Mont Saint-Hilaire, Quebec, and in British Columbia's abundant felsic plutonic rocks. This brilliant gemstone forms in granite pegmatites and can dazzle in shades of yellow and rich golden brown! Though Canada isn't a major source of gem-quality topaz, rockhounds cherish the stunning specimens unearthed in these geological hotspots.
TORCH: The [2024 Summer Olympic Games](https://www.olympics.com/en/olympic-games/paris-2024) start tomorrow in Paris, France! Canada has had the honour of hosting the Olympic Games three times over the years: Montreal (1976), Calgary (1988) and Vancouver (2010). During these historic events, the [Olympic torch relay](https://olympic.ca/2020/02/21/faq-the-olympic-torch-relay/) travelled thousands of kilometres across Canada, passing through cities, towns, and remote regions, symbolizing unity, friendship, and the spirit of the Games. The torch relay provided Canadians from coast to coast with the opportunity to participate in the Olympic excitement and showcase their pride in being part of this global celebration of sport. Whether it's the thrill of the Games or the warmth of the torch, Canada has left an indelible mark on the Olympic movement.
TORTE: Schmoo torte is a Canadian dessert specialty that originated in Winnipeg, Manitoba. A classic schmoo torte consists of layers of sponge cake or angel food cake, whipped cream, nuts, and caramel sauce. The schmoo torte was first invented in 1948 by a Winnipeg mother, Dora Zaslavsky, for her son Murray's Bar Mitzvah.
TRACE: [Leave No Trace Canada](https://leavenotrace.ca/) is a non-profit organization dedicated to promoting outdoor ethics and the seven Leave No Trace principles with the goal of encouraging Canadians to enjoy the benefits of the outdoors while protecting Canada's natural and cultural heritage. The mission of Leave No Trace Canada is to promote and inspire responsible outdoor recreation through science-based education and partnerships throughout Canada.
TRACK: Canada's best summer Olympic sport is athletics, which includes running, hurdles, long jump, high jump, decathlon and other track & field events. Canada has earned 66 medals in athletics since 1900, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 33 bronze.
TRAIN: Canada has a large and well-developed railway system that includes transcontinental freight train services by Canadian National (CN) and Canadian Pacific (CP), and nationwide passenger train services by Via Rail.
TREAT: Happy Halloween from Canuckle! 🎃 While the act of going door-to-door in costume in exchange for something sweet to eat has been around since the Middle Ages, it wasn't until sometime in the last century that people started saying "trick or treat." Trick-or-treating as we know it in Canada began in the late 1920s. In fact, the earliest recorded usage of the phrase “trick or treat” comes from Blackie, Alberta, where in 1927 a newspaper article reported on pranksters demanding “trick or treat” at houses. There is also record of a variation of the phrase originating in Chatsworth, Ontario in 1917, and then appearing in [The Sault Daily Star](https://www.sootoday.com/rooted/origin-of-phrase-trick-or-treat-in-print-traced-to-the-sault-6033664) in Saut Ste. Marie, Ontario on Nov 1, 1917. "Tricks or treats you could hear the gangs call out," the article read. Either way, it has a Canadian origin story that lives on to this day!
TREES: One of the most widely-known facts about Canada is that we’ve got an abundance of trees, but did you know that Canada actually boasts 30 per cent of the world’s boreal forest and 10 per cent of the world’s total forest cover?
TRILL: The common loon’s haunting trill is one of the most recognizable sounds of a Canadian summer. Each male’s trill is unique, functioning as an acoustic fingerprint that announces his size and strength to rival loons listening across the water. Canada is home to roughly 94% of the world’s breeding loon population, making its lakes the heartland of this iconic bird.
TROOP: The Canadian Armed Forces has personnel deployed across Canada and around the world. Since 1947, Canadian troops have completed 72 international missions.
TROUT: With freshwater lakes, rivers and streams covering almost 9% of the country's total area, Canada is a haven for anglers. Canada is home to many different species of trout, including steelhead, rainbow trout, lake trout, brown trout, cutthroat trout and brook trout. Approximately 25% of the world's lake trout lakes are found in the province of Ontario.
TRUCE:
At the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918, a truce was declared to end the First World War. This Armistice marked the beginning of peace after four years of global conflict, and the date became known as [Remembrance Day](https://legion.ca/remembrance/remembrance-day) in Canada. Each year, Canadians pause in silence to honour the courage and sacrifice of those who served, reflecting on the moment the guns finally fell silent. Lest we forget.

You can make a donation to the [Royal Canadian Legion's Poppy Fund](https://www.legion.ca/remembrance/the-poppy-campaign/donate-to-the-poppy-fund) to support Canada’s Veterans and their families, while ensuring Canada never forgets: [legion.ca/donations](https://legion.ca/donations)
TRUNK: Mr. Dressup appeared weekday mornings on CBC for almost 30 years. With his tickle trunk filled with costumes and everyday objects, Mr. Dressup inspired kids - and their parents - to make believe and encouraged imaginations to run wild. Through songs, stories, crafts, drawings and play-acting, Mr. Dressup delivered wholesome entertainment and simple life lessons to preschoolers from 1967 to 1996, followed by a decade of reruns. The documentary "[Mr. Dressup: The Magic of Make-Believe](https://tiff.net/events/mr-dressup-the-magic-of-make-believe)" premieres today at the [2023 Toronto International Film Festival](https://tiff.net/)!
TRUST: The [National Trust for Canada](https://nationaltrustcanada.ca/) is an independent national charity that empowers communities to save and renew heritage places. Heritage places are the backbone of resilient, diverse and sustainable communities: think of historic lighthouses and schools, rural landscapes, Indigenous heritage sites, etc. They work with partners, donors and funders to see heritage places play their part as cornerstones of climate action and social cohesion, and they spark important conversations about Canada at the places our members visit and discover.
TUBER: In celebration of [Canada's Agriculture Day](https://www.foodintegrity.ca/canadas-agriculture-day/) on February 11, 2025, let's shine a spotlight on a classic tuber: the humble potato! A staple in many Canadian comfort foods, potatoes are grown in abundance, with Prince Edward Island leading the charge, producing over 2.5 billion pounds annually. These PEI spuds are essential in dishes like poutine and are also exported worldwide. Whether mashed, fried, or chipped, this versatile Canadian tuber is a cornerstone of Canadian agriculture and a true national treasure!
TUNIC: Did you know that the RCMP's red serge tunic is a symbol of Canadian pride and history? Introduced in the 1870s, the red tunic was part of the uniform for the North-West Mounted Police, the RCMP's predecessor. The bold colour was chosen for its high visibility and as a symbol of authority and strength. Over time, the red serge became a lasting emblem of the RCMP's commitment to service and law enforcement across Canada. Today, it remains an iconic part of their ceremonial dress and is instantly recognized worldwide as a representation of Canada's national identity.
TUYAS: A tuya is a rare type of volcano with a flat top and steep sides, formed when lava erupts through a thick glacier or ice sheet. These unique formations are found in regions where glaciers and volcanic activity occurred simultaneously. One of the most notable tuya regions is the Tuya Volcanic Field in far northern British Columbia, near the border with the Yukon. This area, centered around the Tuya Range, showcases some of the best examples of tuyas in the world.
TWEED: [Tweed, Ontario](https://tweed.ca/) is packed with small-town charm, from North America’s smallest jailhouse to its brightly painted fire hydrants inspired by a Pakistan–Ontario exchange program hosted by Canada World Youth in 1987. The community sits along the Moira River near Stoco Lake, making it a favourite fishing spot — especially for muskie and crappie. Each summer, the town also hosts the Tweed Stampede, Ontario’s largest rodeo, celebrating country music, family fun, and community spirit.
TWICE: April 11th is National Poutine Day, and what better way to enjoy this iconic Canadian dish than with twice-fried potatoes! Most traditional poutine recipes call for the potatoes to be fried twice, creating that perfect balance of crispy on the outside and soft on the inside. This ensures the fries can hold up to the rich gravy and squeaky cheese curds without getting soggy. Whether you stick with the classic or get creative, twice-fried fries are the key to the ultimate poutine experience!
TWINE: Today marks the start of the NHL regular season in North America! In hockey, "twine" is a common slang term for the net, and "tickling the twine" refers to scoring a goal - a thrill that no player delivered more than Canadian hockey legend Wayne Gretzky! Known as "The Great One," Gretzky tickled the twine a jaw-dropping 894 times, setting the record for the most career goals in NHL history.
UDDER: Cows are at the heart of the [Canadian dairy industry](https://dairyfarmersofcanada.ca/), which produces everything from milk and butter to cheese and yogurt. Milk is collected from the udder, the part of the cow where it's stored before being carefully cooled and transported. Canada is home to over 10,000 dairy farms, and its farmers follow some of the highest standards in the world for quality, safety, and animal care. So the next time you pour a glass of milk or bite into a gooey grilled cheese, you can thank a Canadian cow!
ULTRA: [Ray Zahab](https://www.rayzahab.com/) is a Canadian explorer, ultra distance runner, and founder of non-profit [impossible2Possible](https://www.impossible2possible.com/). A recent recipient of the Meritorious Service Cross of Canada, Ray is an Explorer in Residence of the Royal Canadian Geographical Society, and Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. In 2015 Canadian Geographic recognized Ray as one of Canada's Top Explorers. He has ran 17,000+ km across the world's deserts, and unsupported expeditions in some of the coldest places on the planet. From ultra marathons to crossing the Sahara and beyond, Ray's journey has taught him that we can truly exceed any limits we think we might have.
UNCLE: [Mon oncle Antoine](https://www.nfb.ca/film/mon_oncle_antoine_en/) (My Uncle Antoine) is a 1971 French-language Canadian drama film directed by Claude Jutra for the National Film Board of Canada. The film depicts life in a rural mining town in Québec before the Asbestos Strike of 1949. Mon oncle Antoine has twice been voted the greatest Canadian film in the Sight & Sound poll, conducted once each decade. The Toronto International Film Festival placed it first in the Top 10 Canadian Films of All Time three times.
UNION: January 11th is Sir John A. Macdonald Day! Macdonald was the first Prime Minister of Canada and one of the architects of Confederation. He was the dominant creative mind which produced the British North America Act and the union of provinces which became Canada. Both before and after Confederation in 1867, Canada used the United Kingdom's Royal Union Flag, commonly known as the Union Jack.
UNITE: Today is [Commonwealth Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/commonwealth-day.html), a celebration of the global community of nations that are united by shared values, including democracy, peace, and respect for human rights. Canada, as a member of the Commonwealth, plays a key role in this collective effort, working alongside 55 other nations to foster cooperation and development. The Commonwealth is a diverse group, yet its members are united in their commitment to making the world a better place. From humanitarian aid to cultural exchange, Canada continues to work with its Commonwealth partners to build a more just and sustainable future.
UPPER: In Canadian history, Upper Canada (also called Canada West) was the region in Canada now known as Ontario. You can travel back in time to one of Canada's largest living-history sites and experience life in the 1860s at [Upper Canada Village](https://www.uppercanadavillage.com/) near Morrisburg, Ontario.
URSON: The urson, also called the tree-porcupine or bear-porcupine, is Canada's only quill-covered climber! With sharp claws and a sturdy tail for balance, it spends much of its time in trees, nibbling on bark and buds. Despite its slow and gentle nature, this prickly creature is well-defended - its 30,000 barbed quills make predators think twice before getting too close! Found across Canada's forests, the urson is a true expert in both climbing and self-defence.
USHER: The [Usher of the Black Rod](https://sencanada.ca/en/about/usher-black-rod) is a key figure in Canada’s Parliament! This official serves as the personal attendant of the Monarch and the Governor General and is responsible for summoning Members of Parliament to the Senate Chamber during the Speech from the Throne and the opening of Parliament. The role dates back centuries and symbolizes the connection between the Senate and the House of Commons. The Black Rod itself is a ceremonial staff, representing the Usher's authority - one of the many traditions that shape Canada's government!
VERSE: Canada has a rich tradition of poetry, with voices from coast to coast to coast crafting verse that captures the country’s landscapes, cultures, and stories. Each April, [National Poetry Month](https://poets.ca/offerings/programs/npm-mnp/), organized by the League of Canadian Poets, celebrates this creative spirit, bringing Canadian verse to life in communities across the country. The 2026 theme, “Land & Sea,” reflects the deep connection between poetry and place that continues to inspire verse from Canadian writers everywhere.
VILLA: Pelee Island, Ontario is home to [Vin Villa](https://www.vinvilla.com/), Canada’s first commercial winery. Founded in 1866, it helped lay the foundation for Canadian winemaking and gained international attention when one of its wines earned the presitigious Bronze Medallion at the 1878 Paris World’s Fair, marking one of the earliest instances of a North American wine being recognized on the world stage.
VIPER: There are 3 endemic venomous snake species in Canada that fall within the pit viper family: the Western rattlesnake, the Prairie rattlesnake, and the Eastern Massasauga rattlesnake. These pit vipers are equipped with heat-sensing pits that help them hunt small mammals even in the cooler Canadian climate. Though they might seem intimidating, all three rattlesnakes are shy creatures that avoid human contact and play an essential role in controlling rodent populations. Conservation efforts, particularly for the endangered Eastern Massasauga, help protect these unique members of Canada's wildlife. So, next time you think of "viper," remember these important native species, quietly helping keep Canada's ecosystems balanced!
VISON: The vison, or mink, is a small, agile mammal found throughout Canada’s forests and wetlands. Known for its sleek, glossy fur and impressive swimming skills, the vison hunts quietly along rivers and lakes. This clever predator helps keep ecosystems balanced and has long been valued by Indigenous peoples for its role in traditional hunting and trapping.
VISOR: The hockey visor changed the NHL after Canadian defenceman Marc Staal took a puck to the eye in 2013 and narrowly avoided missing the rest of his season. The following year, the league introduced a visor requirement for younger players, marking a major shift in hockey safety while allowing many longtime veterans to continue playing without one.
VISTA: Canada’s stunning scenery and mind-defying vistas are a well-known draw to the country. Rugged mountain ranges, thundering rivers and turquoise lakes surrounded by alpine forests – Canada is an absolute wonder to behold! From sweeping grasslands to crashing ocean tides to craggy snow-covered mountains, Canada’s diverse landscapes offer awe-inspiring vistas for every taste.
VOLTS: Tomorrow marks the start of the [Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League](https://chl.ca/lhjmq/) (QMJHL) regular season in Canada! The [Drummondville Voltigeurs](https://chl.ca/lhjmq-voltigeurs/) (aka "Volts") are a Canadian junior ice hockey team of the QMJHL. The franchise was originally granted for the 1982–83 season, and is based in Drummondville, Quebec, playing its home games at the Centre Marcel Dionne. The team won the QMJHL's President's Cup in 2009 and 2024.
WADER: Hip waders are waterproof boots that let anglers stand waist-deep in rivers and lakes, making fishing in Canada’s great outdoors easier and more comfortable. Whether you’re casting for trout in a mountain stream or trying your luck on a northern lake, waders keep you dry while you reel in the catch of the day. Perfect for fishing and exploring wetlands, waders are a must-have for any Canadian angler ready to get closer to the water!
WAFER: Yesterday was World Chocolate Day! The popular Canadian chocolate bar, "Coffee Crisp," features layers of vanilla wafer and coffee-flavoured cream covered in milk chocolate. It's a unique Canadian treat, and it rarely ventures beyond Canada's borders. The candy has largely been made exclusively for Canadian markets - over 150 million Coffee Crisp bars are produced every year in the Nestlé Canada factory in Toronto. How do Canadians like their coffee? Crisp!
WALKS: Canada has some amazing areas, trails, and parks you can walk, but did you know there are a couple that are among the world’s happiest walks? Inghams, a UK travel company that specializes in active holidays around the lakes and mountains of Europe and Canada, looked at social media posts taken on popular walking trails around the world and used facial detection software to find and compare the size of the smiles captured in the posts, generating a happiness score and providing a tangible measurement of how happy travellers are as they embark on different walks around the world! Two trails in Canada made the list of '[The World's Happiest Walks](https://www.inghams.co.uk/walking-holidays/insider-guides/happiest-walks)', with the Bruce Trail in Tobermory, Ontario and the Canadian Rockies in BC & Alberta coming in with a happiness score of 93.67!
WALLS: The only fortified city north of Mexico, one cannot visit Québec City without admiring the fortified walls and ramparts which were the city's defensive system built between 1608 and 1871.
WAVES: August 30th is National Beach Day! It is estimated that Canada has around 2,000 surfers, and they all get their share of waves on the west (British Columbia) and east (Nova Scotia) coasts and on the Great Lakes (Ontario). The wave-rich region of Tofino, BC played a fundamental role in the development of surfing in the country. The so-called surf capital of Canada is home to a vibrant and active community of cold-water wave riders. Surf's up!
WHELK: Whelks are spiral-shelled sea snails commonly found in the cold waters off Canada's Atlantic coast. These hardy creatures are not only a key part of marine ecosystems but also an important catch in the fishing industry, where they are harvested for their delicate meat and exported worldwide. Indigenous peoples have long valued whelks, using their shells to create tools, jewellery, and even decorative wampum beads. These small but mighty molluscs are a fascinating part of Canada's coastal heritage!
WHITE: Red and white, the colours that adorn the National Flag of Canada, have undeniably come to represent Canada both at home and abroad. Red and white have truly become Canada’s national colours, through common use and collective pride, even if they are not officially enshrined in law. The "Great White North" is one of Canada's nicknames, and also used as the title of a [Second City Television](https://www.secondcity.com/network/category/sctv) (SCTV) comedy sketch featuring our favourite two hosers, [Bob & Doug McKenzie](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X-ZvAVcBIrQ)!
WHORL: June is [National Indigenous History Month](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1466616436543/1534874922512) in Canada, a time to recognize the rich history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis. One of the most frequent motifs in Coast Salish art was also a tool of high cultural importance. The spindle whorl allowed Salish women to weave beautiful textiles of spiritual and social significance. The spindle whorl was used to spin fleece into a thick yarn. It consisted of a small disk (whorl) with a shaft, inserted through a hole in the middle. The shaft was up to four feet long, or 120 cm, while the whorl was up to eight inches across, or 20 cm. The whorl was intricately carved from wood or stone with geometric, animal, or human designs. As the disk spun, the design would mesmerize the spinner, thereby bestowing special powers on the woven material.
WINDS: "Four Strong Winds" is a song written by Ian Tyson and recorded by Canadian folk duo Ian and Sylvia. It was a top 10 single in Canada in 1963. The song has a clear Canadian context and subtext, including an explicit mention of the province Alberta as well as references to long, cold winters. In 2005, CBC Radio One listeners chose this song as the greatest Canadian song of all time, and is considered the unofficial anthem of Alberta.
WINDY: St. John’s tops the list of Canada’s windiest cities. With an average annual wind speed of 24.3 km/h, it feels like the wind is constantly blowing. Southern Alberta is one of the windiest regions in Canada. Second only to St. John’s, Lethbridge gets more days with strong winds than any city in Canada, while Calgary – famous for its Chinook blows – is the windiest large city in Canada.
WINGS: Wings are a Super Bowl staple in Canada. According to Chicken Farmers of Canada, Canadians are expected to eat around 90 million chicken wings on Super Bowl Sunday, making it the country's biggest wing-eating day of the year. Whether they’re saucy, spicy, or extra crispy, wings have become just as much a part of the big game north of the border as the kickoff itself.
WOMAN: Happy International Women's Day! It's a global day to recognize and celebrate women's and girls' social, economic, cultural, and political achievements. It's also a time to raise awareness of the progress made towards achieving gender equality and the work remaining to be done. The 'Day of the Woman' was first proclaimed in 1910 at an international women’s conference in Copenhagen. However, it was only until the United Nations recognized the 8th of March as an official day of celebration in 1978. The Government of Canada's theme for [International Women's Day 2024](https://www.canada.ca/en/women-gender-equality/commemorations-celebrations/international-womens-day.html) is "Invest in women: Accelerate progress". It's a call to action and a reminder that gender equality is one of the most effective ways to build healthier, more prosperous, and more inclusive communities. We all have a role to play in building a future where everyone can reach their full potential!
WOMEN: March 8th is [International Women's Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/women-gender-equality/commemorations-celebrations/international-womens-day.html)! It’s a global day to recognize and celebrate women’s and girls’ social, economic, cultural, and political achievements. It’s also a time to raise awareness of the progress made towards achieving gender equality and the work remaining to be done. The Government of Canada’s theme for International Women’s Day 2023 is "Every Woman Counts". Let’s celebrate the successful Canadian women around us, reminding today’s youth and girls that their dream is within reach.
WORLD: The [Toronto Blue Jays](https://www.mlb.com/bluejays) are back in the spotlight, competing in the 2025 World Series – their first appearance in over three decades! As Canada’s only Major League Baseball team, the Jays carry a nation’s hopes for another championship, just as they did with their historic back-to-back World Series wins in 1992 and 1993. From coast to coast to coast, fans are rallying behind the Blue Jays as they chase another world title for Canada!
WOUND: Established in 1995, [Wounds Canada](https://www.woundscanada.ca/) is a charitable organization dedicated to the advancement of wound prevention and management. Wound Canada's mission is to build a healthier Canada by advancing skin health and excellence in wound management. Learn more at [woundscanada.ca](https://www.woundscanada.ca/)!
WOVEN: Today is [Red Dress Day](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/red-dress-day) in Canada – a day to honour and remember Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women, Girls, and Two-Spirit People (MMIWG2S). The red dresses hanging in windows and trees across the country serve as powerful symbols of those whose lives have been taken and those still missing. Traditional Indigenous clothing is often woven with deep cultural meaning, with intricate designs and patterns that reflect stories, spiritual beliefs, and connections to the land. These garments are more than just clothing – they are a form of storytelling, passed down through generations. On Red Dress Day, the red dresses themselves are a modern reflection of these woven traditions, symbolizing strength, resilience, and the ongoing call for justice.
YIELD: Happy Thanksgiving from Canuckle! Today we celebrate the yield of Canada’s harvest and the farmers who make it possible. From turkeys and potatoes to cranberries, apples and the grains that go into stuffing and pies, Canadian farms help fill Thanksgiving tables with the bounty of the season. We give thanks to the farmers whose yield feeds communities from coast to coast to coast.
